scenario: AITA for being home all day and refusing to cook for my mom? | I'm a female in my senior year of high school and I have a younger sister in grade 10. As most of you know, schools have been closed for a while now and won't reopen for at least another month. My dad gets to work from home, but my mom still has to go out to her office. My school just started online teaching, and we've been getting a lot of assignments to complete. However, my mom expects us to make dinner basically every night because "we're home all day". That really annoyed me because yeah "we're home all day" but we have school work to do. I got upset and asked her why doesn't she cook, since she always finishes work at 5 pm and her office is like 6 minutes from home. Well, once she got home today and saw there was no dinner prepared, she got pissed and started screaming at me how she's so ashamed of us and how we're useless. When I explained how yes we're home all day but doesn't mean we have the whole day off, she got even more mad and said that it doesn't take that long to cook. I refuted by "why don't you cook then?" For more context, my mom is an awful cook. She literally puts no effort into learning or looking up recipes. My dad is an excellent cook. He's tried to teach her before, but she refuses to learn and complains. Before, he would cook for us almost every day, even if he came home late from work (he has a high demanding job so his hours range but he's home 6 pm the EARLIEST, sometimes as late as 9 or even 10 pm. + 30-40 minutes one way commuting). And what does he come home to? Either a low effort flavourless meal from my mom, or my mom sitting on her ass watching TV and asking him what's he's gonna make for dinner. So my dad is forced to make dinner at a late hour so he can eat. More recently, he would just eat fast-food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be on the table. However, he asks if us girls are hungry and offers to cook something for us to eat because he's worried that our mom didn't make us a proper meal. I'm a good cook too (self taught), and I try to help out if I don't have too much homework to do. I did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues etc. Also, my dad does practically all the chores in the house, while my mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV. So AITA for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, my dad ended cooking in the end today.

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. Let me read through the scenario again to make sure I understand it properly.

So, there's a high school senior girl, let's call her Alice, who has a younger sister in grade 10. Their schools have been closed for a while and won't reopen for at least another month. Their dad works from home, but their mom still has to go out to her office. The school just started online teaching, and they've been getting a lot of assignments to complete. 

Now, the mom expects them to make dinner every night because "we're home all day." Alice got annoyed because even though they're home all day, they have schoolwork to do. She asked her mom why she doesn't cook since she finishes work at 5 pm and her office is only 6 minutes from home. The mom got upset and started screaming at her, saying she's ashamed of them and that they're useless. Alice explained that just because they're home all day doesn't mean they have the whole day off, and her mom got even more mad, saying it doesn't take that long to cook. Alice retorted by asking why her mom doesn't cook then.

From the context, it seems like the mom is an awful cook. She doesn't put any effort into learning or looking up recipes. The dad, on the other hand, is an excellent cook and has tried to teach her before, but she refuses to learn and complains. Before, the dad would cook for them almost every day, even if he came home late from work. He has a high-demanding job, so his hours vary, but he's home at 6 pm earliest, sometimes as late as 9 or even 10 pm, plus 30-40 minutes one way commuting. So, he's often exhausted when he gets home. 

The mom, however, either makes a low-effort, flavourless meal or sits on her ass watching TV and asks him what he's going to make for dinner. So, the dad is forced to make dinner at a late hour so he can eat. More recently, he would just eat fast food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be on the table. However, he asks if the girls are hungry and offers to cook something for them because he's worried that their mom didn't make them a proper meal.

Alice is also a good cook, self-taught, and she tries to help out if she doesn't have too much homework. She did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues, etc. Also, the dad does practically all the chores in the house, while the mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV.

So, the question is: Is Alice AITA (Am I The Ass) for not cooking dinner today and telling her mom not to expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, her dad ended up cooking in the end today.

Alright, so I need to evaluate whether Alice's action is morally acceptable or not. Let's break this down.

First, let's consider the expectations. The mom expects Alice and her sister to cook dinner every night because they're home all day. However, Alice and her sister are in high school, dealing with online school and assignments. They have responsibilities and tasks to complete, just like their parents do.

Alice is a good cook and has been helping out, but she also has her own schoolwork to manage. It's reasonable for her to feel overwhelmed when her mom expects her to cook every night on top of her schoolwork.

The mom, on the other hand, is not contributing much to the household chores or cooking. She either makes low-effort meals or doesn't cook at all, leaving the responsibility to the dad, who already has a demanding job and is exhausted when he comes home. The dad ends up cooking for the family, which adds to his workload.

So, when Alice refused to cook dinner today and told her mom not to expect dinner every time she comes home, she was standing up for herself and asserting her boundaries. She's recognizing that she has her own responsibilities and that it's unfair for her mom to expect her to handle all the cooking without any help.

It's also worth noting that the mom's behavior seems unreasonable. She's expecting her daughters to cook every night but isn't contributing herself. She's also not improving her cooking skills despite her husband's attempts to teach her. This creates an imbalance in the household responsibilities.

Alice's refusal to cook dinner today can be seen as a form of self-care and setting boundaries. She's acknowledging that she has her own tasks and that it's not fair for her to take on all the cooking responsibilities without support.

However, it's also important to consider the impact of her actions on the family dynamic. By refusing to cook, she might be contributing to the tension in the household, especially since her dad ended up cooking in the end. It's possible that her mom feels disrespected or that the family is not working together as a team.

But, given the context, it seems like the mom has been setting unrealistic expectations and not pulling her weight. Alice is just one person, and it's not fair for her to be the sole provider of meals every night, especially when she has her own responsibilities.

In conclusion, while Alice's refusal to cook might have caused some tension, it's a reasonable response to the unfair expectations placed on her by her mom. She's asserting her boundaries and recognizing her own responsibilities, which is a mature and necessary step in managing her time and workload.
